hard_gates.gate: G1 tenant isolation: my own live attack as tenant A (alnoor) on tenant B (gulfsteel) through the API, exports, jobs and files
hard_gates.evidence:
attack/attack.mjs collected 872 ids that belong only to B. As A it then sent:
- all 261 operations with B's ids
- 1,668 documented query-parameter requests
- 1,155 tenant-switch requests (headers, query, cookies)
- 190 export requests, 77 filter requests and 349 path-variant and audit requests

B's rows were unchanged by A's attack (md5 of every tenant table, b-before/after).

The script flagged 138 answers. My controls in attack/probe.txt show every one is benign:
- The 54 audit-record answers with B ids are byte-identical to answers for a random id.
- Every switched answer is identical to the same request sent plainly. 'Gulf Steel' and 'الخليج' are A's own contact 'Gulf Steel Industries FZE'.
- The B tenant id in A's audit CSV is an echo: A's own job payload {tenantId: B}, written by the attacker.
- After A's DELETEs, B still has its rate and file. A gets 404 on B's file.

The full tenant export of A (32 files, 14.9 MB) contains none of the 33 B values I searched for (attack/full-export.txt).

hard_gates.gate: G1 tenant isolation: the database role the app uses
hard_gates.evidence:
No erp role is superuser or has BYPASSRLS. All 34 tables with tenant_id have:
- row-level security enabled and forced
- tenant_id NOT NULL
- an owner other than erp_app

erp_app can reach no table without tenant_id (db-roles.txt).

As erp_app (db-app-role-attack.txt):
- With no tenant set it sees 0 contacts, users and audit rows.
- With A bound it sees 0 B rows. UPDATE of B contacts changes 0 rows. DELETE is denied. Moving an A contact to B violates the RLS policy.
- A session-level tenant without the transaction stamp sees 0 rows.
- erp_app cannot disable RLS ('must be owner').

biggest_gap.title: The permissions gate (G2) cannot see a missing second-level permission check inside an answer: a user who may change users but not read them reads users' audit history, and all 101 G2 tests pass
biggest_gap.detail:
G2 checks each endpoint's declared permission: grant exactly one, deny the rest. Many answers also make a second, in-handler decision through the kernel's ICurrentUser.Has. Examples:
- which record kinds the audit log shows
- whether a job's output text is included
- which job kinds may be scheduled or rerun
- whether a list view may be shared

I planted two faults in ICurrentUser.Has, p00's own kernel. Both are real faults, and no hard gate saw them:
- P24c: a record kind's read permission is implied by any permission on that resource, for the audit reader. A user holding identity.users.update and audit.log.read, without identity.users.read, reads the administrator's user-record history. Users' history holds e-mails and names. All 101 G2 tests pass, the 13 audit gate tests pass and the 23 audit module tests pass.
- P24b: jobs.jobs.output is implied by jobs.jobs.read. G2 misses it. Only p12's own module test catches it.

So a second-level permission check stays safe only while each module remembers to write its own test for it. For a UAE trading company, the audit trail is the place a restricted clerk must not read colleagues' records. The bar says 'every action is denied unless a role grants it'.

The real product is clean (the probe passes unplanted), so this is a gate gap for the backlog, not a block.
biggest_gap.evidence:
Plant: plants/plants.diff, P24b and P24c in src/Kernel/Erp.Kernel/Security/SessionAuthentication.cs.

Results: plants/plant-results.txt and the logs plant-G2-P24b.log, plant-JOBS-P24b.log, plant-G2-P24c.log, plant-AUDIT-P24c.log, plant-AUDITGATE-P24c.log, plant-PROBE-P24c.log and plant-PROBE-NONE.log.

The probe test is CRITIC_PROBE_P24c_... in tests/Erp.Modules.Audit.Tests/AuditTrailTests.cs (in plants.diff). Under P24c it fails with 'Assert.Equal() Failure: Expected: 0 Actual: 1'. Unplanted, it passes.

1. Apply plants.diff.
2. Run dotnet test tests/Erp.Gates.Tests --filter FullyQualifiedName~Erp.Gates.Tests.G2 with CRITIC_PLANT=P24c: 101 passed.
3. Run the probe with CRITIC_PLANT=P24c: it fails.

other_findings: The share rebalance (this round's own change) did not shorten the long share in a real run. The measured-family table deals four shares of about 7,020 predicted seconds each (my simulation from the live OpenAPI inventory: share-dealing-simulation.txt). In the verify, though, G1HttpIsolationShardTests took 28 m 53 s, 35 m 4 s, 1 h 5 m and 33 m 9 s; r23 had the third share at 1 h against 30 to 38 min. The dotnet stage is still paced by one share (7,112 s), and wall time is 8,503 s against r23's 8,639 s and the 3,600 s quiet-machine figure. The measured family seconds are summed request time across concurrent requests, not a share's wall time, so they cannot predict which share runs longest.

Reliability improved: 1 of 1 alone verify passed, against 1 of 3 in r23. The new wait covers only the two builds, though: 'builds over after waiting 30 s (load 7.97)'. Vitest and the harness self-tests then ran beside the three .NET test groups, at load up to about 21, the same class of load that broke clientIsolation in r23. They passed this time.

Processor-time accounting, for the owner's information: the ratchet's verify.cpuSeconds counts only the toolbox containers. The machine was busy 59,565 s over the run, and 34,584 s of that (58.1 %) was outside the counted stages: the PostgreSQL test containers, as docs/decisions/p00-foundation-request-cost.md records. r23 showed the same, at 57.3 %.
